title: CSA CCSK v5 (Certificate of Cloud Security Knowledge)

nodes.title: Part 1: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 1. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: Under the shared responsibility model for a typical IaaS deployment, which area is ALWAYS the cloud customer's responsibility regardless of the provider?
flashcards.back: In any IaaS deployment the customer owns everything from the guest OS upward — patching, configuration, application code and data. The provider always owns the physical facility, the host hypervisor and the supporting power/cooling/network plant. CSA emphasises that drawing this line correctly is the foundation of every cloud control discussion.

flashcards.front: Several government agencies with similar mission and compliance requirements share a single cloud infrastructure operated for their exclusive use. Which NIST SP 800-145 deployment model best describes this arrangement?
flashcards.back: NIST defines a community cloud as infrastructure provisioned for exclusive use by a specific community of consumers from organisations that share concerns (mission, security, policy, compliance). Public is open to anyone, private serves one organisation, and hybrid is the composition of two or more separate deployment models bound by portable data or applications.

flashcards.front: A developer wants to upload code that runs on demand, with the provider transparently handling the OS, runtime and autoscaling, and billing only for execution time. Which service model best fits?
flashcards.back: Serverless function platforms such as AWS Lambda and Azure Functions are categorised by CSA as a form of PaaS: the customer supplies only code while the provider manages the runtime, scaling and underlying OS. IaaS still exposes the guest OS to the customer, SaaS is a finished application, and 'DaaS' is not part of the NIST service-model taxonomy.

flashcards.front: In CSA's logical model of cloud computing, the management plane, APIs and identity controls that orchestrate cloud resources belong to which layer?
flashcards.back: CSA's logical model separates infrastructure (the underlying compute/storage/network), metastructure (the management plane and APIs), applistructure (the applications) and infostructure (the data). The metastructure is unique to cloud — there is no equivalent on-premises — and is a high-value attack surface because compromising it can pivot to every other layer.

questions.q: Under the shared responsibility model for a typical IaaS deployment, which area is ALWAYS the cloud customer's responsibility regardless of the provider?
choices: Operating system patching and application configuration on the customer's instances
Physical security of the underlying data center facility
Hypervisor patching and host-OS hardening on the compute hosts
Power, cooling and undersea-cable redundancy of the provider's network
questions.explanation: In any IaaS deployment the customer owns everything from the guest OS upward — patching, configuration, application code and data. The provider always owns the physical facility, the host hypervisor and the supporting power/cooling/network plant. CSA emphasises that drawing this line correctly is the foundation of every cloud control discussion.

questions.q: Several government agencies with similar mission and compliance requirements share a single cloud infrastructure operated for their exclusive use. Which NIST SP 800-145 deployment model best describes this arrangement?
choices: Public cloud (open to the general public)
Community cloud (shared by organisations with common concerns)
Private cloud (provisioned for a single organisation)
Hybrid cloud (a composition of two or more distinct clouds)
questions.explanation: NIST defines a community cloud as infrastructure provisioned for exclusive use by a specific community of consumers from organisations that share concerns (mission, security, policy, compliance). Public is open to anyone, private serves one organisation, and hybrid is the composition of two or more separate deployment models bound by portable data or applications.

questions.q: A developer wants to upload code that runs on demand, with the provider transparently handling the OS, runtime and autoscaling, and billing only for execution time. Which service model best fits?
choices: Infrastructure as a Service (customer manages the guest OS)
Software as a Service (provider delivers a complete application)
Platform as a Service, including serverless function platforms
Data as a Service (provider exposes managed datasets)
questions.explanation: Serverless function platforms such as AWS Lambda and Azure Functions are categorised by CSA as a form of PaaS: the customer supplies only code while the provider manages the runtime, scaling and underlying OS. IaaS still exposes the guest OS to the customer, SaaS is a finished application, and 'DaaS' is not part of the NIST service-model taxonomy.

questions.q: In CSA's logical model of cloud computing, the management plane, APIs and identity controls that orchestrate cloud resources belong to which layer?
choices: Infrastructure (physical and virtual compute, storage and network)
Infostructure (data and information assets)
Applistructure (applications and services consuming the platform)
Metastructure (management plane and APIs that bind the others)
questions.explanation: CSA's logical model separates infrastructure (the underlying compute/storage/network), metastructure (the management plane and APIs), applistructure (the applications) and infostructure (the data). The metastructure is unique to cloud — there is no equivalent on-premises — and is a high-value attack surface because compromising it can pivot to every other layer.

nodes.title: Cloud governance: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Governance is the set of policies and guardrails that keep a cloud account safe and on-budget as it scales from one engineer to a hundred. Think tagging standards, budget alerts, organizational policies, and the multi-account strategy.

flashcards.front: Why use multiple accounts (an Organization) instead of one big account?
flashcards.back: Blast-radius isolation: a compromised prod account doesn't leak into dev. Billing clarity: per-team or per-environment cost reports. Quota independence: prod doesn't share API limits with sandbox. Service Control Policies (AWS) / management groups (Azure) enforce 'no one can disable CloudTrail' across the whole org.

flashcards.front: What is a Service Control Policy (SCP)?
flashcards.back: An AWS Organizations policy that sets the maximum permissions any IAM identity in a member account can have. Even if a user's IAM policy grants `s3:*`, an SCP denying `s3:DeleteBucket` overrides it. SCPs are guardrails, not grants — they only restrict.

flashcards.front: Tagging strategy — name three high-leverage tags.
flashcards.back: (1) Owner / team — who pays and who to page. (2) Environment (prod/staging/dev) — drives access controls and lifecycle. (3) Cost-center / project — for chargeback. Tags are free and infinitely valuable for cost allocation and automation; enforce them with policies.

A pre-baked multi-account setup with security baselines: org with master + audit + log-archive + workload accounts, CloudTrail / Config enabled everywhere, SSO wired up, network templates ready. AWS Control Tower / Azure Landing Zones / GCP setup automate this so you start on a safe foundation, not bare cloud.

questions.q: An auditor wants to review a cloud provider's self-attestation against the Cloud Controls Matrix using a publicly searchable registry. Which CSA artifact should they consult?
choices: The CAIQ submission published in the CSA STAR Registry
A SOC 2 Type II report issued by an independent CPA firm
An ISO/IEC 27001 certification statement from an accredited body
A FedRAMP authorisation package stored in the GSA marketplace
questions.explanation: The CSA STAR Registry hosts Consensus Assessments Initiative Questionnaire (CAIQ) responses aligned to the Cloud Controls Matrix — free and publicly searchable. SOC 2, ISO/IEC 27001 and FedRAMP are valuable assurance artefacts but are issued by other bodies, not CSA, and access is not necessarily public.

questions.q: A security team discovers that thousands of permissions granted to users and machine identities across AWS, Azure and GCP have never actually been used. Which capability is purpose-built to discover and right-size these entitlements?
choices: Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM)
Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management (CIEM)
Cloud Workload Protection Platform (CWPP)
Secure Access Service Edge (SASE)
questions.explanation: CIEM tools specialise in discovering, analysing and reducing identity entitlements across cloud platforms — the canonical control for unused or over-privileged permissions. CSPM focuses on configuration drift, CWPP on workload runtime protection, and SASE on identity-aware network access at the edge.

questions.q: An architecture team wants east-west traffic between workloads inside the same VPC to be denied by default, allowing only flows that match explicit identity-aware policies. Which approach best meets this requirement?
choices: Coarse-grained ACLs applied at the VPC perimeter only
A single shared security group attached to every workload in the VPC
Microsegmentation with default-deny policies between workloads
An edge web application firewall with signature-based blocking
questions.explanation: Microsegmentation places identity-aware, fine-grained controls between individual workloads so lateral movement is denied by default. VPC perimeter ACLs and a shared security group are too coarse to stop east-west traffic, and a WAF only inspects north-south HTTP requests to a public-facing application.

questions.q: A platform team decides that no running instance will ever be patched in place. When a vulnerability is found, the team rebuilds the golden image and redeploys. Which workload-security practice is being applied?
choices: Live in-place kernel patching with kpatch or ksplice
Configuration-management drift remediation on existing hosts
Agent-based hot patching of binaries on the running instance
Immutable infrastructure — replace, never modify, running instances
questions.explanation: Immutable infrastructure forbids changes to a running instance: the fix lives in a new image, and the instance is replaced. The other three options all modify the running host, which preserves drift and undermines the immutability invariant CSA recommends for cloud workloads.

nodes.title: Software supply-chain security: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Software supply-chain security protects everything that goes into building and delivering software — third-party dependencies, build pipelines, and published artifacts — because attackers increasingly compromise the supply chain instead of the app directly. Exams cover SBOMs, dependency risk, signing and provenance, and pipeline hardening.

flashcards.back: A Software Bill of Materials — a complete inventory of every component, library, and dependency in a piece of software, including versions. It lets you quickly answer 'are we affected?' when a new vulnerability (like Log4Shell) drops, instead of guessing what's inside your builds.

flashcards.front: What are typosquatting and poisoned dependencies?
flashcards.back: Typosquatting publishes a malicious package with a name nearly identical to a popular one (e.g., a one-letter difference), hoping you install it by mistake. A poisoned dependency is a legitimate package that's been compromised to inject malicious code into everyone who pulls it. Both attack you through trusted package ecosystems.

flashcards.front: What do artifact signing and provenance provide?
flashcards.back: Signing (e.g., with Sigstore/cosign) cryptographically proves an artifact came from a trusted publisher and wasn't tampered with. Provenance is verifiable metadata about how and where an artifact was built. Frameworks like SLSA define maturity levels for trustworthy, tamper-resistant build pipelines.

flashcards.front: How do you secure the CI/CD pipeline itself?
flashcards.back: Treat the pipeline as a high-value target: lock down build runners, scope credentials to least privilege and prefer short-lived tokens over stored secrets, pin and verify dependencies, isolate build steps, and require code review. A compromised build server can sign and ship malware as if it were legitimate.

questions.q: A regulated organisation stores sensitive data with a SaaS provider but wants the ability to revoke access to that data unilaterally by destroying the encryption key. Which key-management approach delivers this control?
choices: Bring Your Own Key, with the master key held in a customer-controlled KMS
Provider-managed server-side encryption using the SaaS provider's default keys
AES-256 at-rest encryption certified to FIPS 140-3
Transparent Data Encryption configured by the SaaS provider
questions.explanation: BYOK lets the customer supply and rotate the master key — and crucially destroy it — so that revoking the key renders the data cryptographically inaccessible even to the provider. Provider-managed keys leave revocation entirely to the provider, and AES-256 / TDE describe algorithms or mechanics rather than who holds custody of the key.

questions.q: Which control most directly reduces the risk that tampered or unauthorised code reaches production through a continuous-delivery pipeline?
choices: Quarterly penetration tests of the production environment
Cryptographically signed commits and container images verified at deploy time
Network intrusion-prevention at the production VPC ingress
Disabling interactive SSH access on all production hosts
questions.explanation: Signing artefacts (commits with Sigstore/GPG, container images with cosign or Notary) and verifying signatures at deploy time blocks unsigned or tampered artefacts from being released — the supply-chain control CSA prescribes for pipeline integrity. Pen-tests, IPS and SSH lockdown harden the runtime but do not establish trust in the build chain.

questions.q: What is the most distinctive forensic challenge of investigating a security incident in a public cloud compared with an on-premises data centre?
choices: Inability to run any endpoint or anti-malware tooling on cloud workloads
Complete absence of provider-side audit logs for tenant activity
Loss of physical access and reliance on provider APIs for hypervisor-level evidence
Encryption that prevents any capture of volatile memory from cloud hosts
questions.explanation: Tenants cannot physically seize hardware or read host memory in a public cloud; they depend on provider APIs and provider-controlled logs for hypervisor-level evidence — the central forensic constraint CSA highlights. Endpoint tools and memory snapshots do work in cloud, and providers expose extensive audit logs (CloudTrail, Azure Activity Log, GCP Cloud Audit Logs).

questions.q: Which statement best captures the core principles of Zero Trust as it applies to cloud architectures (per NIST SP 800-207 and CSA guidance)?
choices: Trust traffic originating inside the corporate network and verify only at the perimeter
Replace identity-based access with a site-to-site VPN between offices and the cloud
Use IP allowlisting instead of identity controls to keep policy simple and fast
Verify explicitly, enforce least privilege, and assume breach for every request
questions.explanation: Zero Trust as defined by NIST SP 800-207 and reinforced in CCSK v5 rests on three pillars: verify explicitly, enforce least privilege, and assume breach. Internal-network trust is removed, VPNs are typically replaced by identity-aware proxies / ZTNA, and IP allowlisting is treated as a weak signal that supplements — not replaces — identity controls.
